# Components

<!-- Generated by `pnpm components` from the design system's source. Don't edit it by hand. -->

## Diagram

`import Diagram from "@artifactory/design-system/diagram";`

A diagram written in D2 and drawn at build time: systems, processes, flows, hierarchies and
relationships between named parts. For a drawing D2 can't express, such as a plot, a cell or a
timeline, write an SVG and use `Figure`.

Put the `.d2` file next to the entry, import it, and pass it as `src`:

```mdx
import fluxo from "./fluxo.d2";

<Diagram
  src={fluxo}
  alt="O sangue sai do coração pelas artérias e volta pelas veias."
  caption="A circulação sistêmica: do coração ao corpo e de volta."
/>
```

D2 draws in its own theme colours, and each becomes a design system colour, so diagrams follow
the site in light mode, dark mode and print. "Colours in diagrams" lists which token each one
becomes, to explain how a diagram looks: a D2 file can't choose them. Code labels are ink, with
grey comments.

D2 also draws in the design system's style: labels are Archivo, condensed like the page's
headings, and rectangles, squares and containers are drawn with square corners whatever
`style.border-radius` says, so leave that out. Code labels, `sql_table` and `class` members and
`style.font: mono` are set in D2's own monospace. The page numbers each diagram by its section
("Diagrama 4.1").

The check fails a file that asks for what the design system doesn't draw: colours written in
the file (`style.fill`, `style.stroke` or `style.font-color` as `"#…"` or a colour name),
`style.shadow`, `style.fill-pattern`, `style.animated`, `style.opacity` below 1, `sketch`, a legend
(`vars.d2-legend`), and a `link`, `tooltip` or `icon`, or a link in a markdown label. Say it in
the prose instead.

The layout engine is ELK; a file may choose `dagre` or `tala` with
`vars: { d2-config: { layout-engine: dagre } }`.

### Props

- `src` (`string`, required): The diagram, imported from a `.d2` file next to the entry.
- `alt` (`string`, required): What the diagram shows, in a sentence or two. Screen readers read it instead of the drawing.
- `caption` (`string`, optional): One short sentence under the diagram, after its number ("Diagrama 4.1"), saying what to look
  for. Leave it out when the paragraph before already says it.

## Figure

`import Figure from "@artifactory/design-system/figure";`

A hand-written SVG drawing: plots, cells, apparatus, geometry, timelines, and anything else D2
can't express. For boxes and arrows, write D2 and use `Diagram`.

Put the `.svg` file next to the entry, import it with `?raw`, and pass it as `src`:

```mdx
import celula from "./celula.svg?raw";

<Figure
  src={celula}
  alt="Uma célula animal com núcleo, mitocôndrias e membrana."
  caption="As organelas de uma célula animal, fora de escala."
/>
```

Colour the drawing with the `fill-` and `stroke-` classes under "Colours in figures", which
follow the site in light mode, dark mode and print. Shapes and text without a fill are drawn in
the text colour, and text uses the face of the page's headings. The page numbers each figure by
its section ("Figura 4.1"). Colours written in the file (`fill="#…"`) don't
follow dark mode, so leave them out.

### Props

- `src` (`string`, required): The drawing, imported with `?raw` from an `.svg` file next to the entry.
- `alt` (`string`, required): What the drawing shows, in a sentence or two. Screen readers read it instead of the drawing.
- `caption` (`string`, optional): One short sentence under the drawing, after its number ("Figura 4.1"), saying what to look for.
  Leave it out when the paragraph before already says it.

## Note

`import Note from "@artifactory/design-system/note";`

A margin note on one paragraph: a remark, a caveat or a pointer that would interrupt the sentence
if it stood in it. On a wide screen it sits in the right margin, level with its paragraph's
first line; on narrower screens it folds behind a "Note" marker ("Nota" in Portuguese) at the
end of the paragraph, which opens it under the paragraph. Keep it to a sentence or two of plain
text, inline math or inline code.

Put it at the very end of a paragraph of the main text, right after the last word with no space
before it, and give each paragraph one note at most. Never put one in a question, a list or a
heading. For text the owner must read, write it in the paragraph instead.

```mdx
import Note from "@artifactory/design-system/note";

A transformada é a integral de $y(t)e^{-st}$ de zero ao infinito.<Note>A integral começa em zero: o que acontece antes de $t = 0$ não conta.</Note>
```

### Props

None: what goes between its tags is its content.

## NumericQuestion

`import NumericQuestion from "@artifactory/design-system/numeric-question";`

An auto-checked question whose answer is a single computed number. The owner works it out, types
the number and presses Check, and the question locks and shows right or wrong once the answer is
saved. A wrong answer also shows the right one, with its unit and tolerance. Prefer it to
`SingleChoice` whenever options would let the owner rule some out or work backwards from them
instead of computing. Ask one number per question: a vector's components or a quadratic's two
roots are one question each ("the smaller root", "the larger root").

The owner may write `,` or `.` as the decimal separator, a sign, `e` notation (`6,02e23`) or a
fraction (`3/4`), but no thousands separators, `π`, `√` or expressions. Input that isn't a
number gets a message and uses up nothing. Without a tolerance the check is exact, so give one
that matches the computation's precision whenever the answer is rounded.

Write the question inside it. It can hold math, code and lists:

```mdx
import NumericQuestion from "@artifactory/design-system/numeric-question";

<NumericQuestion id="queda-livre" answer="9.81" tolerance={0.01} unit="m/s²">

Uma pedra cai 4,905 m em 1 s a partir do repouso. Qual é a aceleração $g$?

</NumericQuestion>
```

### Props

- `id` (`string`, required): The question's ID: readable kebab-case, unique within the artifact and never reused, even
  after the question is removed. The owner's answers belong to it, and `#q-<id>` links to it.
- `answer` (`string`, required): The right number, as a string with `.` as its separator: `"9.81"`, `"-3/4"`, `"6.02e23"`. A
  fraction stays exact, and the right answer shows it as written, in the page's convention.
- `tolerance` (`number`, optional): How far from `answer` a right answer may be, inclusive: with `0.01`, `9.80` to `9.82` are right
  for `"9.81"`. Give this or `relativeTolerance`, not both.
- `relativeTolerance` (`number`, optional): How far from `answer` a right answer may be, as a fraction of it: `0.01` is 1 %. For an answer
  whose size makes a fixed tolerance meaningless. It can't be used when `answer` is zero.
- `unit` (`string`, optional): The unit, in plain Unicode text (`"m/s²"`, `"mol⁻¹"`, `"°C"`), shown beside the field. The
  owner types only the number.

## OpenQuestion

`import OpenQuestion from "@artifactory/design-system/open-question";`

A self-checked question: the owner answers in their own words, reveals the model answer, and
marks their answer right or wrong themselves. The model answer opens once something is written,
and opening it fixes what was written; the mark saves the answer and locks the question. Use it for explanations, derivations and proofs, where there's no single
answer the artifact could check. When the answer is one of a few options, use `SingleChoice`;
when it's a single computed number, use `NumericQuestion`.

Write the question, a blank line, `---`, another blank line, then the model answer. Without the
blank line above it, `---` turns the question into a heading. Both can hold math, code and lists:

```mdx
import OpenQuestion from "@artifactory/design-system/open-question";

<OpenQuestion id="por-que-pi-r2">

Por que a área do círculo é $\pi r^2$?

---

Some os anéis de raio $\rho$ e largura $\mathrm{d}\rho$: $\int_0^r 2 \pi \rho \, \mathrm{d}\rho = \pi r^2$.

</OpenQuestion>
```

### Props

- `id` (`string`, required): The question's ID: readable kebab-case, unique within the artifact and never reused, even
  after the question is removed. The owner's answers belong to it, and `#q-<id>` links to it.

## Proof

`import Proof from "@artifactory/design-system/proof";`

The proof of a theorem, lemma or corollary written as a `Statement`. It is unnumbered: it opens
with a run-in "Demonstração." / "Proof." and its last line ends with a small square, so the owner
sees where the argument stops. Write it right after the statement it proves. A proof anywhere
else opens with what it proves, linked ("Demonstração do Teorema 2.1."), so write it elsewhere
only when the subject proves the result later. A definition has no proof.

Write it at the top level of a section, like its statement: nested in a list or a question, a
proof never counts as following its statement, so it always opens by naming it, and its equations
go unnumbered. Its content is ordinary Markdown (paragraphs, math, lists), with a blank line after
the opening tag and before the closing one. Don't write "Demonstração", "Proof" or an end mark in
the text: the page writes them.

```mdx
import Proof from "@artifactory/design-system/proof";
import Statement from "@artifactory/design-system/statement";

<Statement kind="lemma" id="fermat">

Se $f$ tem um extremo em $c \in (a, b)$ e é derivável em $c$, então $f'(c) = 0$.

</Statement>

<Proof of="fermat">

Num máximo em $c$, o quociente $\frac{f(c + h) - f(c)}{h}$ é $\le 0$ para $h > 0$ e $\ge 0$ para
$h < 0$, então o limite, $f'(c)$, é $0$.

</Proof>
```

### Props

- `of` (`string`, required): The `id` of the theorem, lemma or corollary it proves.

## Ref

`import Ref from "@artifactory/design-system/ref";`

A citation of a `Statement` in the same artifact. It reads as the statement's label and number
in the artifact's main language ("Teorema 2.1" / "Theorem 2.1") and links to it. The page counts
the number, so a citation stays right when statements or paragraphs move. Write the article or
preposition around it yourself, and never write the label or number by hand. Cite paragraphs,
equations and figures by their numbers in the prose instead ("pela equação (2)").

```mdx
import Ref from "@artifactory/design-system/ref";

A prova usa o <Ref to="fermat" /> e a <Ref to="derivavel" />.
```

### Props

- `to` (`string`, required): The `id` of the statement it cites.

## SingleChoice

`import SingleChoice from "@artifactory/design-system/single-choice";`

An auto-checked question with one right option among several. The owner picks an option and
presses Check, and the question locks and shows right or wrong once the answer is saved. A
wrong answer also ticks the right option. The page letters the options a), b), c), so don't
letter them yourself. Use it when exactly one option is right and the options can be read side
by side. For a computed number, use `NumericQuestion`, since options would let the owner work
backwards from them.

Write the question first, then the options as one numbered list at the end. Options can hold
inline math and code, one paragraph each:

```mdx
import SingleChoice from "@artifactory/design-system/single-choice";

<SingleChoice id="derivada-de-x2" answer={2}>

Qual é a derivada de $x^2$?

1. $x$
2. $2x$
3. $x^2 / 2$

</SingleChoice>
```

### Props

- `id` (`string`, required): The question's ID: readable kebab-case, unique within the artifact and never reused, even
  after the question is removed. The owner's answers belong to it, and `#q-<id>` links to it.
- `answer` (`number`, required): The number of the right option in the list, counting from 1.

## Stage

`import Stage from "@artifactory/design-system/stage";`

A part of the artifact that computes in the browser: an algorithm run from the start the owner
picks, or a function traced on the numbers they type. Use it only when no component can do the
job: a fixed sequence of steps is a `Stepper`, and anything that asks the owner something and
records the answer is a question. A Stage is a block in the page, numbered on the figures'
series ("Figura 4.1"), and a page may hold several, each with its own build.

You write two things:

- **The content as written**, between the Stage's tags and in `figure`: a drawing, tables, one
  fenced code block and prose, as ordinary Markdown. The page shows it before the owner chooses,
  without JavaScript and in print, so write it to make sense with no step on it. With `choose` it
  is the starting state; with `input` it is the first example's result.
- **A custom build**, a `<build>.build.ts` file next to the entry, which turns the option the
  owner chose, or the numbers they typed, into steps. It imports only
  `@artifactory/design-system/stage-build` (below), and holds no CSS, colours, HTML or DOM
  code, and nothing that outlives a reload.

The Stage draws the rest: the row of options or the fields and Start, the step counter and
arrows, the line that says each step, the number and the caption, for the keyboard, screen
readers, the phone, dark mode and print. A drawn part whose `data-part` is an option's name also
chooses that option when clicked or tapped. That's a shortcut for the pointer: the options stay
the way in for the keyboard and screen readers, so the part takes no focus. Any element or `<g>`
will do, and the Stage gives it a hit area of at least 44px.

````mdx
import Stage from "@artifactory/design-system/stage";
import grafo from "./grafo.svg?raw";

<Stage
  build="prim"
  choose={{ label: "Começar em", options: ["A", "B", "C"] }}
  prompt="Escolha um vértice para começar."
  figure={grafo}
  alt="Um grafo com três vértices e três arestas com pesos."
  caption="O algoritmo de Prim a partir do vértice escolhido."
>

| Vértice | Chave | Pai |
| ------- | ----: | --- |
| A       |     ∞ | —   |
| B       |     ∞ | —   |
| C       |     ∞ | —   |

</Stage>
````

```ts
// prim.build.ts
import { defineBuild, type Step } from "@artifactory/design-system/stage-build";

export default defineBuild({
  steps(start) {
    const steps: Step[] = [];
    steps.push({
      say: `Começa em ${start}, com chave 0.`,
      parts: { [start]: "reversed" },
      rows: { [start]: "reversed" },
      cells: [{ row: start, column: "Chave", text: "0", mark: "strong" }],
    });
    // …one whole step per pass of the algorithm
    return steps;
  },
});
```

**Typed input.** Give `input` instead of `choose` when the owner types whole numbers, such as
a function's arguments. The fields open filled with the first example, and the content as
written must be that example's result: `pnpm check` fails when a table as written isn't what
the first example's last step leaves in it. A step shows the content as written with only what
it names applied, so every step must name every cell whose value differs from that result, or
the answer shows mid-run; no check catches that. Without JavaScript and in print, where the
fields don't show, the Stage names the first example in their place, after the input's label
("Calcular mdc(a, b) a = 48, b = 18"), so the prose needn't. Type the build's input with the
fields' names. This one traces a function line by line, marking the line each step runs:

````mdx
<Stage
  build="mdc"
  input={{
    label: "Calcular mdc(a, b)",
    fields: [
      { name: "a", min: 1, max: 9999 },
      { name: "b", min: 0, max: 9999 },
    ],
    examples: [{ a: 48, b: 18 }, { a: 18, b: 48 }, { a: 7, b: 0 }],
  }}
  prompt="Digite dois números e comece."
  caption="O algoritmo de Euclides, linha por linha."
>

```python
def mdc(a, b):
    while b != 0:
        a, b = b, a % b
    return a
```

| Variável | Valor |
| -------- | ----: |
| a        |     6 |
| b        |     0 |

</Stage>
````

```ts
// mdc.build.ts
import { defineBuild, type CellChange, type Step } from "@artifactory/design-system/stage-build";

export default defineBuild<{ a: number; b: number }>({
  steps(input) {
    let { a, b } = input;
    const values = (mark?: "strong"): CellChange[] => [
      { row: "a", column: "Valor", text: String(a), mark },
      { row: "b", column: "Valor", text: String(b), mark },
    ];
    const steps: Step[] = [
      {
        say: `mdc recebe a valendo ${String(a)} e b valendo ${String(b)}.`,
        lines: { 1: "reversed" },
        cells: values("strong"),
      },
    ];
    while (b !== 0) {
      steps.push({
        say: `b vale ${String(b)}, não zero: o laço roda.`,
        lines: { 2: "reversed" },
        cells: values(),
      });
      const say = `a passa a ${String(b)} e b ao resto de ${String(a)} por ${String(b)}, ${String(a % b)}.`;
      [a, b] = [b, a % b];
      steps.push({ say, lines: { 3: "reversed" }, cells: values("strong") });
    }
    steps.push({ say: "b vale 0: o laço acaba.", lines: { 2: "reversed" }, cells: values() });
    steps.push({
      say: `Devolve a: o mdc é ${String(a)}.`,
      lines: { 4: "reversed" },
      rows: { a: "reversed" },
      cells: values(),
    });
    return steps;
  },
});
```

The last step of `{ a: 48, b: 18 }`, the ninth, leaves `a` at 6 and `b` at 0, as the table is
written. Put the example worth looking at first, since `pnpm look` shoots only the first, and add
entries to `input.examples` for the edges, such as a zero. The page refuses a number that isn't
whole or is out of bounds with the bounds in the step's line, and draws its field dashed.

**Steps are whole.** `steps` returns every step for that option or those numbers, at least one
and at most 200. The Stage starts each step from the content as written and applies only what it
names, so name everything the step shows, not what changed since the step before. A build that
throws, or gives more than 200 steps, is refused in the step's line: with `input`, a typed number
the examples never tried can reach a bug the check never saw, and the page keeps working.

**Code.** Write the code as one fenced code block between the Stage's tags, with its language,
as anywhere else: it keeps its highlighting and line numbers, so never put code in a table. A
step marks its lines with `lines`, by number from 1 as the page numbers them. Mark the line the
step runs `reversed`, and only that one: the Stage draws it as a bar of ink across the code's
whole width, even where a long line scrolls sideways, and announces the step as "Passo 3 de 9.
Linha 3. …". A step with no `reversed` line is announced without one. The other marks work on
lines too, by the same meanings: `strong` sets a line at 600, `dashed` draws it in a dashed box
and `muted` greys it whole, such as the branch an `if` didn't take.

**A table that grows.** A step's `body` replaces the table's rows, so a teste de mesa gains a row
each time the loop runs, as one written by hand does. Each row is a list of cell texts, one per
column, and takes the look of the last row as written, so write at least one row of the kind the
build adds. `rows` and `cells` then find the rows `body` wrote, by their first cell, so give each
row a first cell of its own, such as the pass's number. The Stage must hold exactly one table, so
a table of current values and a teste de mesa each take a Stage of their own, one after the
other, each with its build. Since steps are whole, give every step its whole `body`, so going
back shows the rows that step had. With `choose` a step without one shows the rows as written,
the starting state; with `input` they're the whole result, so once a run gives `body` on one
step, it gives it on every step, `[]` for no rows. Print and the page without JavaScript show
the rows as written, so with `input` write the table as the first example's last step leaves
it, every row included. This one traces a loop line by line, a row per pass:

````mdx
<Stage
  build="fatorial"
  input={{
    label: "Calcular fatorial(n)",
    fields: [{ name: "n", min: 0, max: 12 }],
    examples: [{ n: 4 }, { n: 0 }, { n: 12 }],
  }}
  prompt="Digite um número e comece."
  caption="O teste de mesa de fatorial(n), uma linha por passagem do laço."
>

```python
def fatorial(n):
    f = 1
    while n > 1:
        f = f * n
        n = n - 1
    return f
```

| Passagem |  n |  f |
| -------- | -: | -: |
| início   |  4 |  1 |
| 1        |  3 |  4 |
| 2        |  2 | 12 |
| 3        |  1 | 24 |

</Stage>
````

```ts
// fatorial.build.ts
import { defineBuild, type Step } from "@artifactory/design-system/stage-build";

export default defineBuild<{ n: number }>({
  steps(input) {
    let { n } = input;
    let f = 1;
    let row = "início";
    const body = [[row, String(n), String(f)]];
    const steps: Step[] = [];
    const step = (line: number, say: string, wrote?: "n" | "f") => {
      steps.push({
        say,
        lines: { [line]: "reversed" },
        // A copy: the loop goes on changing `body` after this step.
        body: body.map((cells) => [...cells]),
        cells: wrote === undefined ? [] : [{ row, column: wrote, mark: "strong" }],
      });
    };
    step(2, `f começa em 1, e n vale ${String(n)}.`, "f");
    while (n > 1) {
      step(3, `n vale ${String(n)}, mais que 1: o laço roda.`);
      const was = f;
      f = f * n;
      row = String(body.length);
      const cells = [row, String(n), String(f)];
      body.push(cells);
      step(4, `f passa a ${String(f)}, ${String(was)} vezes ${String(n)}.`, "f");
      n = n - 1;
      cells[1] = String(n);
      step(5, `n passa a ${String(n)}.`, "n");
    }
    step(3, `n vale ${String(n)}, não mais que 1: o laço acaba.`);
    steps.push({
      say: `Devolve f: o fatorial é ${String(f)}.`,
      lines: { 6: "reversed" },
      body,
      rows: { [row]: "reversed" },
    });
    return steps;
  },
});
```

Step 3 of `{ n: 4 }` adds the row `1`, with f at 4 in bold and n still at 4, and step 4 sets
that row's n to 3 in bold. The last, the twelfth, leaves the four rows as the table is written,
the row `3` reversed.

**Marks** mean the same in the drawing, the tables and the code. Choose them by meaning: `strong`
for what is settled or just changed, `dashed` for what is provisional, such as a candidate,
`muted` for what is no longer available, and `reversed` for the one current thing. Give every
element or `<g>` the build marks a `data-part` name, and colour it with the classes under
"Colours in figures", since each mark acts only on some of them, on the part and inside it:

- `strong` thickens shapes with a `stroke-` class and sets labels (`<text>`) in bold.
- `dashed` dashes shapes with a `stroke-` class.
- `muted` turns the `-text` and `-accent` colours grey, and labels with no fill of their own.
- `reversed` swaps ink and ground: `-surface` turns to ink, and `-text`, `-accent` and labels
  with no fill of their own turn to the ground. Draw a part the build reverses as a
  `fill-surface stroke-text` shape with an unclassed label.

Anything else stays as drawn, such as a shape filled with `fill-muted` or `fill-tint`, or a
label with a `fill-` class of its own, so a vertex filled that way can't be reversed. A mark on
a part with nothing it acts on fails the check.

**Tables** are found by their text: a row by its first cell, a column by its header, as the
page shows them with the formatting dropped, so a first cell `*a*` is the row `a`. Write first
cells and headers as plain words or symbols, without math. Keep each row's first cell and each
header unique among the Stage's tables, since a name that matches more than one fails the
check. A part and a row may share a name: `parts` marks only the drawing, and `rows` only the
tables.

**Beside the drawing.** A Stage sets its tables under its drawing. Set `beside` only where the
owner must see a step's marks and its table's rows together to follow the step, such as a graph
and its table of keys and parents, which stacked sit a scroll apart; most Stages leave it out.
With `beside`, on a wide screen, the tables sit beside the drawing when the Stage holds `figure`
and only tables between its tags, and both fit at their own widths: the drawing's width, 24px
and the widest table's width come to 680px or less, as a 425px graph beside a table of keys and
parents does. Otherwise, and always on a phone, a tablet and paper, the tables sit under the
drawing. Code or prose between the tags keeps everything under the drawing, so write the prose
about the Stage before or after it. With `choose`, write the table's cells as wide as any step
makes them (∞, NIL), so it stays beside on every step. With `body` or `input`, a step's cells
exist only when it runs, so a step whose cells come out wider puts the table under the drawing
for that step.

**Say it for the ear.** `say` is read aloud after "Passo N de M. Linha L.": write operators in
words ("o resto de 48 por 18", not "48 % 18"; "b não é zero", not "b != 0"), since a screen
reader reads `%` as "por cento" and other operators symbol by symbol.

`pnpm check` runs the build on every option or example against the built page and fails on a
throw, no steps, more than 200, a step that isn't shaped like a `Step`, an empty `say`, a part,
row, column or code line the content doesn't have, a mark that changes nothing in its part,
`lines` in a Stage without exactly one code block, more than one `reversed` line, `body` in a
Stage without exactly one table or with no row as written, a `body` row without one text per
column, or, with `input`, a step without `body` in a run whose other steps give it, or tables as
written that aren't the first example's result, a row the last step adds or drops included. The
page refuses the same runs.

### Props

Give one of these 2 sets of props.

With `choose`:

- `choose` (`{ label: string; options: string[] }`, required): What the owner chooses before the run: the label over the options, and the options, each a
  short word or symbol, such as a vertex's name. `steps` gets the option chosen. On a 393px
  phone, seven one-letter options fit on one line under the label; more, or longer names, wrap.
- `build` (`string`, required): The custom build: the name of the `<build>.build.ts` file next to the entry.
- `prompt` (`string`, required): What to do first, shown where each step's line will be: "Escolha um vértice para começar."
- `figure` (`string`, optional): A drawing the build marks, imported with `?raw` from an `.svg` file next to the entry. Name
  each part the build marks with `data-part`.
- `alt` (`string`, optional): What the drawing shows as written, in a sentence or two. Give it with `figure`.
- `beside` (`boolean`, optional): Sets the tables beside the drawing on a wide screen, as "Beside the drawing" below says. Set
  it sparingly, only where a step's marks and its rows must be seen together; most Stages
  stack. Give it with `figure`.
- `caption` (`string`, optional): One short sentence under the Stage, after its number ("Figura 4.1").

With `input`:

- `input` (`{ label: string; fields: { name: string; label?: string; min: number; max: number }[]; examples: Record<string, number>[] }`, required): What the owner types before the run: the label over the fields, and one field per whole
  number, with the `name` `steps` gets it by, a `label` to show instead of the name, and the
  smallest and largest number it takes. `steps` gets `{ [name]: number }`. `examples` are
  inputs, each giving every field a whole number in its bounds, and `pnpm check` runs the build
  on every one. The first fills the fields as written, so write the content as its result:
  each table as its last step leaves it. The page refuses a number that isn't whole or is out
  of bounds, and numbers the build throws on.
- `build` (`string`, required): The custom build: the name of the `<build>.build.ts` file next to the entry.
- `prompt` (`string`, required): What to do first, shown where each step's line will be: "Escolha um vértice para começar."
- `figure` (`string`, optional): A drawing the build marks, imported with `?raw` from an `.svg` file next to the entry. Name
  each part the build marks with `data-part`.
- `alt` (`string`, optional): What the drawing shows as written, in a sentence or two. Give it with `figure`.
- `beside` (`boolean`, optional): Sets the tables beside the drawing on a wide screen, as "Beside the drawing" below says. Set
  it sparingly, only where a step's marks and its rows must be seen together; most Stages
  stack. Give it with `figure`.
- `caption` (`string`, optional): One short sentence under the Stage, after its number ("Figura 4.1").

### The build: `@artifactory/design-system/stage-build`

A build file imports only this module. Its default export is `defineBuild({ steps(choice) { … } })` with `choose`, or `defineBuild<{ a: number; b: number }>({ steps(input) { … } })` with `input`.

#### `Mark`

The four marks a step can put on the drawing, the tables and the code, named for what they
mean. The Stage draws each one the same way everywhere:

- `strong`: settled, or just changed. A thicker line, or text at 600.
- `dashed`: provisional, such as a candidate. A dashed line, or a cell or code line in a dashed
  box.
- `muted`: no longer available, such as a branch not taken. The grey.
- `reversed`: the one current thing. A shape filled with ink and its label in the ground, a
  reversed cell, or the running code line as a bar of ink across the code's width.

```ts
type Mark = "strong" | "dashed" | "muted" | "reversed";
```

#### `CellChange`

A change to one table cell, found by its row and its column.

- `row` (`string`, required): The row, by the text of its first cell.
- `column` (`string`, required): The column, by the text of its header.
- `text` (`string`, optional): The cell's text in this step, as plain text: Markdown and math show as typed, so write a
  symbol in Unicode ("∞"). Leave it out to keep the cell as written.
- `mark` (`Mark | undefined`, optional): The cell's mark in this step, over its row's. Leave it out to keep the row's mark.

#### `Step`

One step of the run, whole: the Stage starts it from the content as written and applies only
what it names, so name everything this step shows, not what changed since the last one.

- `say` (`string`, required): What this step did, in one sentence in the artifact's language. The Stage shows it beside the
  counter, and screen readers hear it after "Passo N de M." and, when a line is marked
  `reversed`, "Linha L.", so it must make sense without the drawing.
- `parts` (`Record<string, Mark>`, optional): Marks on the drawing's parts, by their `data-part` name.
- `lines` (`Record<number, Mark>`, optional): Marks on the code block's lines, by line number from 1, as the page numbers them. Mark the line
  this step runs `reversed`, and only that one: the Stage says "Linha L." before `say`. The Stage
  must hold exactly one fenced code block.
- `body` (`string[][]`, optional): The table's body rows in this step, in place of the rows as written: one list of cell texts
  per row, one text per column, as plain text like `CellChange.text`. Each row takes the look of
  the last row as written. `rows` and `cells` then find rows among these, not the rows as
  written. Leave it out to keep the rows as written, with `choose` only: with `input` the rows as
  written are the first example's result, so a run that gives `body` on one step gives it on
  every step, `[]` for no rows, or the page refuses it. The Stage must hold exactly one table, with
  at least one row as written. Give each step its own lists, `body.map((cells) => [...cells])`,
  since a step keeps the lists it's given, and a later change to them reaches it too.
- `rows` (`Record<string, Mark>`, optional): Marks on whole table rows, by the text of their first cell.
- `cells` (`CellChange[]`, optional): New text and marks on single table cells.

#### `Typed`

What the owner typed into a Stage's `input`: each field's whole number, by the field's `name`.

```ts
type Typed = Record<string, number>;
```

#### `Build`

A custom build: what turns the owner's choice into steps. With `choose`, `steps` gets the option
as text; with `input`, it gets each field's number, typed as `Input`.

- `steps` (`(input: Input) => Step[]`, required): Every step for the option the owner chose or the numbers they typed, in order, at least one
  and at most 200. Called again from step 1 whenever they choose again or press Start.

#### `defineBuild`

Wraps the build so TypeScript checks it. A `.build.ts` file's default export. With `input`,
give the fields' names as its type, `defineBuild<{ a: number; b: number }>({ … })`, so `steps`
gets them typed: `pnpm check` fails when they aren't the Stage's fields.

```ts
function defineBuild<Input extends string | Typed = string>(build: Build<Input>): Build<Input>;
```

## Statement

`import Statement from "@artifactory/design-system/statement";`

A definition, theorem, lemma, corollary or worked example, numbered by the page as a clause of
its section so that it can be cited ("Teorema 2.1"). Its number stands in the margin in the
paragraphs' series, its label runs in at the start of its first line ("**Teorema** (Valor
médio)."), and a theorem, lemma or corollary reads in italic while a definition or example stays
upright. Use it for each definition or result the subject names and the owner should be able to
cite, and for each worked example: a problem solved in full, with its solution shown openly after
"Solução." / "Solution.". An example teaches; when the owner should work the problem out
themselves, ask it as a question instead (`OpenQuestion`, `NumericQuestion`). Keep explanations in
paragraphs, and asides in a `Note`. Cite it anywhere in the artifact with `Ref`.

Write it at the top level of a section, after the first `##` heading: never inside a list, a
question or another component. Its content is ordinary Markdown (paragraphs, math, lists, and in
an example tables and figures too, which keep the page's numbering), with a blank line after the
opening tag and before the closing one. Don't write the kind, the number or the name in the
text: the page writes them. In a definition, set the defined term in bold. In an example, write
the problem, a blank line, `---`, another blank line, then the solution, as in an
`OpenQuestion`'s model answer; never write "Solução" yourself. Only an example has a `---`.

```mdx
import Statement from "@artifactory/design-system/statement";

<Statement kind="definition" id="derivavel" name="Função derivável">

Uma função $f$ é **derivável** em $(a, b)$ quando $f'(x)$ existe para cada $x \in (a, b)$.

</Statement>

<Statement kind="theorem" id="valor-medio" name="Valor médio">

Se $f$ é contínua em $[a, b]$ e derivável em $(a, b)$, então $f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$ para algum $c \in (a, b)$.

</Statement>

<Statement kind="example" id="valor-medio-parabola" name="Uma parábola">

Onde, em $(0, 2)$, a tangente a $f(x) = x^2$ é paralela à secante de $0$ a $2$?

---

A secante tem inclinação $\frac{4 - 0}{2 - 0} = 2$ e $f'(c) = 2c$, então $c = 1$.

</Statement>
```

### Props

- `kind` (`"definition" | "theorem" | "lemma" | "corollary" | "example"`, required): What it states. The page writes the kind's label in the artifact's main language
  ("Definição", "Teorema", "Lema", "Corolário", "Exemplo" / "Definition", "Theorem", "Lemma",
  "Corollary", "Example").
- `id` (`string`, required): The statement's ID: readable lowercase kebab-case, unique among the artifact's statements.
  `<Ref to="…">` cites it, and `#S-<id>` links to it.
- `name` (`string`, optional): The name the subject gives it, in plain text, shown in parentheses after the label
  ("Teorema (Valor médio)."). Leave it out when it has none.

## Stepper

`import Stepper from "@artifactory/design-system/stepper";`

Steps the owner through a mechanism, a diagram or a code walkthrough one step at a time, with
back and forward buttons above it. Use it when the order is the point: the stages of a process,
a drawing built up part by part, or a program read a few lines at a time. For a picture that
reads at once, use `Diagram` or `Figure`.

Give it exactly one of `diagram`, `figure` or `lines`:

````mdx
import mitose from "./mitose.d2?steps";
import bomba from "./bomba.svg?raw";

<Stepper diagram={mitose} alt="As quatro fases da mitose." captions={["Prófase", "Metáfase", "Anáfase", "Telófase"]} />

<Stepper figure={bomba} alt="A bomba de sódio e potássio em três tempos." captions={["A bomba prende três Na⁺.", "Ela os solta fora da célula.", "Ela traz dois K⁺ para dentro."]} />

<Stepper lines={["1", "2-3", "5"]} captions={["Recebe o raio.", "Calcula a área.", "Devolve."]}>

```ts
…
```

</Stepper>
````

A D2 diagram steps through its `steps` boards, each drawn as a whole, in one frame the size of
the largest board: write every board so it reads on its own. Diagrams and drawings take their
colours as in `Diagram` and `Figure`. A stepper needs at least two steps, and `captions`, when
given, needs one caption per step.

Printed, a stepper shows every step: each board under its number and caption, and code with each
step's lines and caption listed under it. A figure prints once, at its last step, with the
captions listed under it, so make the last step the complete drawing.

### Props

Give one of these 3 sets of props.

With `diagram`:

- `diagram` (`string[]`, required): The diagram's boards, imported with `?steps` from a `.d2` file next to the entry. The root
  board is the first step, unless everything is drawn under `steps`, and each board in `steps`
  is the next.
- `alt` (`string`, required): What the drawing shows as a whole, in a sentence or two. Screen readers read it.
- `captions` (`string[]`, optional): One short caption per step, in step order, shown beside the buttons. Screen readers announce
  it with the step number and, for code, the step's lines; without captions they hear only
  those. Leave it out only when the prose around the stepper already explains each step.

With `figure`:

- `figure` (`string`, required): The drawing, imported with `?raw` from an `.svg` file next to the entry. Each element with a
  `data-step` shows only in the steps it lists: `data-step="2"` in step 2, `"2-4"` in steps 2 to
  4, `"2-"` from step 2 to the end, and `"1, 3"` in steps 1 and 3. Elements without one always
  show. The highest step number named is the number of steps.
- `alt` (`string`, required): What the drawing shows as a whole, in a sentence or two. Screen readers read it.
- `captions` (`string[]`, optional): One short caption per step, in step order, shown beside the buttons. Screen readers announce
  it with the step number and, for code, the step's lines; without captions they hear only
  those. Leave it out only when the prose around the stepper already explains each step.

With `lines`:

- `lines` (`string[]`, required): The lines each step highlights, one entry per step, counting lines from 1: `"3"`, `"3-5"`,
  `"3-"` (line 3 to the end) or `"1-2, 6"`. The other lines turn grey. Put one fenced code block
  inside the stepper, with blank lines around it.
- `captions` (`string[]`, optional): One short caption per step, in step order, shown beside the buttons. Screen readers announce
  it with the step number and, for code, the step's lines; without captions they hear only
  those. Leave it out only when the prose around the stepper already explains each step.

## Colours in diagrams

D2 draws with its theme's colours, which a D2 file can't choose. The design system replaces each with a token:

- `--color-text`: N1, B1, B2, AA2
- `--color-text-muted`: N2, N3
- `--color-border`: N4, N5, B3
- `--color-surface-subtle`: N6, B4, B5, AA4, AA5, AB4, AB5
- `--color-surface`: N7, B6

## Colours in figures

Each class paints an SVG element with a token:

- `fill-text`: `--color-text`
- `fill-muted`: `--color-text-muted`
- `fill-accent`: `--color-text`
- `fill-tint`: `--color-surface-subtle`
- `fill-surface`: `--color-surface`
- `fill-border`: `--color-border`
- `stroke-text`: `--color-text`
- `stroke-muted`: `--color-text-muted`
- `stroke-accent`: `--color-text`
- `stroke-tint`: `--color-surface-subtle`
- `stroke-surface`: `--color-surface`
- `stroke-border`: `--color-border`

The `text`, `muted` and `accent` classes are ink: use them for lines and labels. The `tint`, `surface` and `border` classes are too faint to read on the page: use them for fills and gridlines, never for text or a line that carries meaning, unless it sits on an ink fill.
